items.title: Early Greek Contact with India
items.body:
## First Contact

- India's interaction with the Greeks began with the invasion of **north-western India by Alexander (327–325 BC)** — the first significant contact between the two cultures.
- After Alexander's death, his general **Seleucus Nicator** established rule from **Turkey to the Indus River**.
- **Chandragupta Maurya defeated Seleucus Nicator**, leading to a **marriage alliance** — a diplomatic, peaceful resolution.
- **Bindusara** maintained good relations with **Antiochus I of Syria**, strengthening Mauryan–Seleucid ties.
- **Ashoka's Rock Edict 13** mentions **five Yona/Yavana kings**, showing deep and enduring India–Greek ties.
- Mauryan administrative institutions are believed to have been influenced by **Persian and Greek systems**.
- Trade flourished — India exported **ivory, pearls, indigo**, and aromatics like **spikenard and malabathrum**.
keyPoints: First major India–Greek contact = Alexander's invasion of NW India (327–325 BC).
Seleucus Nicator ruled from Turkey to the Indus; defeated by Chandragupta Maurya, sealed by a marriage alliance.
Bindusara kept good relations with Antiochus I of Syria.
Ashoka's Rock Edict 13 names five Yona/Yavana kings.
Exports to the Greek world: ivory, pearls, indigo, spikenard, malabathrum.
items.mnemonic: Contact chain — 'Alexander → Seleucus → Chandragupta → Bindusara → Ashoka' = A-S-C-B-A.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Indo-Greek Invasion (Early Greek Contact with India)

items.title: The Indo-Greek Kingdom — Extent & Origin
items.body:
## Who Were the Indo-Greeks?

- The **Indo-Greek Kingdom** — also called **Indo-Bactrians** or the **Yavana Kingdom** — ruled the **north-western Indian subcontinent**, including **Afghanistan, Pakistan, and parts of Iran**.
- It began with the invasion by **Demetrius I around 180 BCE**, following the **decline of the Mauryan Empire**.
- Their heartland (**Bactria**) controlled the trade routes linking **Gandhara** with the West.

figure.alt: Map showing the extent of the Indo-Greek Kingdom and the possible extent of its expeditions
figure.caption: Indo-Greek Kingdom (green) covering the north-west with centres at Sagala, Taxila and Pushkalavati; expeditions (pink) reached towards Mathura and Pataliputra.

keyPoints: Also known as Indo-Bactrians or the Yavana Kingdom.
Ruled NW subcontinent: Afghanistan, Pakistan, parts of Iran.
Founded by Demetrius I's invasion c. 180 BCE after the Mauryan decline.
Bactria controlled trade routes between Gandhara and the West.
items.mnemonic: Three names for one realm — 'Indo-Greek = Indo-Bactrian = Yavana'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Indo-Greek Invasion (Indo-Greek Invasion overview)

items.title: Causes of the Indo-Greek Invasion
items.body:
## Why the Greeks Invaded

- **Weakening of the Seleucid Empire:** after **250 BCE** the Seleucid Empire disintegrated; Emperor **Antiochus III conquered Kabul**, laying the foundation for the Greek invasion of India.
- **Bactrian independence:** **Bactria and Parthia** gained independence from the Syrian Empire during the **3rd century BCE**.
- **Domino from Central Asia:** **Scythian tribes**, displaced by the building of the **Great Wall of China**, pushed towards Greek and Parthian territories, encouraging the **Bactrian Greeks to invade India**.
keyPoints: Seleucid Empire weakened after 250 BCE; Antiochus III took Kabul.
Bactria and Parthia broke away from the Syrian Empire in the 3rd century BCE.
Scythians displaced by the Great Wall of China pushed into Greek/Parthian lands.
This displacement pushed the Bactrian Greeks southward into India.
items.mnemonic: Three triggers — 'Weak Seleucids, Free Bactria, Pushy Scythians'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Indo-Greek Invasion (Causes of Indo-Greek Invasion)

items.title: Demetrius — The Bactrian Invader
items.body:
## Demetrius Enters India

- **Demetrius I** was the **son of Euthydemus**, a **Greco-Bactrian king**.
- He **invaded Afghanistan and Punjab** and extended his rule across **north-western India** (c. **180 BCE**).
- **Demetrius II (180 BCE)** is named as the **first known Indo-Greek king**:
  - Came into **conflict with Pushyamitra Shunga**.
  - Extended **Bactrian rule south of the Hindu Kush**.
  - Issued **bilingual square coins** (Greek and Kharosthi).
keyPoints: Demetrius I = son of the Greco-Bactrian king Euthydemus.
Invaded Afghanistan and Punjab, extending rule over NW India c. 180 BCE.
Demetrius II is named the first known Indo-Greek king.
Clashed with Pushyamitra Shunga; pushed Bactrian rule south of the Hindu Kush.
Issued bilingual square coins in Greek and Kharosthi.
items.mnemonic: Demetrius = 'Down through the Hindu Kush' — first to push Bactrian rule south.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Indo-Greek Invasion (Demetrius I; Rulers of the Indo-Greek Kingdom)

items.title: Menander I (Milinda) — The Most Notable Ruler
items.body:
## Menander I — Soter, the 'Savior'

- The **most important Indo-Greek ruler** (c. **165/145–130 BCE**), described as **Soter** or **"Savior"**.
- Ruled from the **Kabul Valley to Western Uttar Pradesh**, with his capital at **Sakala (modern Sialkot, Pakistan)**.
- Expanded to the **Swat Valley** and **Kabul River Valley**; led a **successful expedition to Mathura** and **attacked Pataliputra** (without consolidating control there).
- **Converted to Buddhism** under the sage **Nagasena**.
- Famous for **coinage** featuring **Greek gods and Buddhist symbols** (Lotus, Wheel); his coinage covers the **largest geographical area** of any Indo-Greek ruler.
keyPoints: Most important Indo-Greek king; titled Soter ('Savior').
Ruled Kabul Valley to Western UP; capital at Sakala (Sialkot).
Campaigned to Mathura and attacked Pataliputra but did not consolidate control.
Converted to Buddhism under Nagasena.
Coinage (Greek gods + Buddhist Lotus/Wheel) covers the largest area of any Indo-Greek ruler.
items.mnemonic: Menander = 'Milinda, Soter of Sakala' — the Savior king who turned Buddhist.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Indo-Greek Invasion (Menander I – The Most Notable Indo-Greek Ruler)

items.title: Milinda Panho & Nagasena
items.body:
## Questions of Milinda

- The **Milinda Panho** (**"Questions of Milinda"**) is a **Buddhist text** recording a **dialogue between Menander (Milinda) and the sage Nagasena**.
- Under **Nagasena's influence**, Menander **converted to Buddhism**.
- The text stands as key evidence of the **Indo-Greek engagement with Buddhist philosophy** and of Greek rulers patronising Indian religion.
keyPoints: Milinda Panho = 'Questions of Milinda', a Buddhist dialogue text.
It records the discussion between Menander (Milinda) and Nagasena.
Nagasena's teaching led Menander to convert to Buddhism.
Prime evidence of Indo-Greek engagement with Buddhist thought.
items.mnemonic: 'Milinda asks, Nagasena answers' — the Milinda Panho dialogue.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Indo-Greek Invasion (Conversion to Buddhism; Milinda Panho)

items.title: Antialcidas & the Heliodorus Pillar (Besnagar/Vidisha)
items.body:
## The Garuda-Dhvaja at Vidisha

- King **Antialcidas** sent his emissary **Heliodorus** to the court of **Bhagabhadra**.
- Heliodorus **erected a Garuda-Dhvaja (Garuda pillar) at Vidisha (Besnagar)**, **dedicated to Lord Vishnu**.
- Heliodorus, a Greek ambassador, **adopted Vaishnavism** — one of the **earliest instances of Vaishnavism in Indian epigraphy**.

figure.alt: Map of the Indo-Greek Kingdom with major centres including Vidisha region
figure.caption: Indo-Greek and neighbouring territory: Heliodorus's Garuda pillar stood at Vidisha (Besnagar), in the court of Bhagabhadra.

keyPoints: Antialcidas's emissary was Heliodorus, sent to king Bhagabhadra.
Heliodorus raised a Garuda-Dhvaja (Garuda pillar) at Vidisha/Besnagar.
The pillar was dedicated to Lord Vishnu; Heliodorus adopted Vaishnavism.
One of the earliest epigraphic records of Vaishnavism in India.
items.mnemonic: 'Heliodorus → Garuda → Vishnu at Vidisha' — a Greek who became a Vaishnava.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Indo-Greek Invasion (Antialcidas; Cultural Contributions)

items.title: Indo-Greek Coinage — Gold & Portrait Coins
items.body:
## A Numismatic Revolution

- The Indo-Greeks were the **first to issue gold coins in India**, used for **larger transactions**.
- Their **bilingual coins** carried **Greek and Kharosthi scripts**, easing trade and cultural exchange between India and Greece.
- Coins depicted **Greek deities** such as **Athena, Apollo, and Zeus** alongside **Indian religious symbols** like the **Dharmachakra**, the **bull**, and the **elephant**.
- They are also credited with the first well-executed **portrait coins** bearing the ruler's likeness (e.g., Menander), a Hellenistic practice new to India.

figure.alt: Composite of Gandhara-style Buddha sculpture and bilingual Indo-Greek coins
figure.caption: Indo-Greek legacy: Gandhara-style Buddha imagery and bilingual (Greek + Kharosthi) coins bearing rulers' portraits and deities.

keyPoints: First rulers to issue gold coins in India (for larger transactions).
Bilingual coins in Greek + Kharosthi scripts aided trade.
Depicted Greek gods (Athena, Apollo, Zeus) with Indian symbols (Dharmachakra, bull, elephant).
Introduced well-crafted portrait coins showing the ruler's likeness.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Indo-Greek Invasion (Coins; Introduction of Gold Coins)

items.title: Art, Religion & the Gandhara School
items.body:
## Hellenistic–Indian Fusion

- Indo-Greek art showcased a **Hellenistic and Indian cultural fusion**, visible in the remains of cities like **Sakala, Ai-Khanoum, and Taxila**.
- The fusion of Greek and Indian styles produced the **Gandhara School of Art**, which depicted the **Buddha in the Graeco-Roman style**.
- The Indo-Greeks **promoted Buddhism**, helping the development of **Mahayana Buddhism** and **Bhakti traditions**.

figure.alt: Gandhara-style seated Buddha with Graeco-Roman drapery beside Indo-Greek coins
figure.caption: Gandhara School: the Buddha rendered in a Graeco-Roman style — the artistic contact-point of Greek and Indian traditions.

keyPoints: Hellenistic–Indian fusion seen at Sakala, Ai-Khanoum, and Taxila.
Produced the Gandhara School of Art — Buddha in Graeco-Roman style.
Indo-Greeks promoted Buddhism, aiding Mahayana and Bhakti traditions.
Coins mixed Greek deities with Buddhist symbols (Lotus, Wheel).
items.mnemonic: Gandhara = 'Greek hands, Buddhist face' — Graeco-Roman Buddha.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Indo-Greek Invasion (Art, Ideology, and Religion; Gandhara School)

items.title: Key Contributions & Decline
items.body:
## Legacy and End

### Key Contributions
- **Cultural exchange:** amalgamation of Greek and Indian traditions in **art, coinage, and religious thought**.
- **Religious influence:** significant role in spreading **Buddhism** and influencing **Mahayana** doctrines.
- **Art & architecture:** a rich legacy of **coinage, sculpture, and architecture**, above all the **Gandhara School**.
- Broadly, contact introduced **Hellenistic** elements — advanced **coin technology** and **Greek terms/astronomy** — into Indian learning.

### Decline
- The empire diminished after **Menander I's death in 130 BCE**.
- **Scythians (Shakas)**, pushed by the **Yuezhi**, invaded Bactria and Indo-Greek territory from the **mid-2nd century BCE**.
- **Internal power struggles**, external attacks, and **decline of trade routes** strained the economy.
- The last Indo-Greek ruler, **Strato II**, ruled until **55 BCE (or 10 AD)**; eventually the **Kushanas** and other powers took over.
keyPoints: Legacy: cultural exchange in art, coinage and religious thought.
Advanced coinage, Gandhara sculpture, and Hellenistic/Greek terms entered Indian learning.
Decline began after Menander I's death (130 BCE).
Scythians (Shakas), pushed by the Yuezhi, overran Bactria and Indo-Greek lands.
Last ruler Strato II (until 55 BCE / 10 AD); Kushanas eventually took over.
items.mnemonic: Decline drivers — 'Shakas + Splits + Shrinking trade' after Menander.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Indo-Greek Invasion (Key Contributions; Decline of Indo-Greek Rule)
